title: Cracking Wordle: How Information Theory Wins 99% of the Time
summary: Wordle players, take note: a mathematical approach developed at Binghamton University can solve the daily puzzle with a staggering 99% success rate. The strategy, published in the Northeast Journal of Complex Systems, harnesses Shannon entropy — a concept from information theory that measures uncertainty. Instead of guessing words with common letters like "ARISE," the method selects guesses that maximize information gain, effectively splitting the remaining possibilities into the smallest possible groups. "A subtle but important insight is that a guess doesn't have to be the most likely answer; it simply has to be informative," explains Donald Stephens, a doctoral student and co-author. The approach can seem counterintuitive because it sometimes suggests obscure words. But by focusing on reducing uncertainty rather than directly hitting the target, the solver often reaches the answer in fewer attempts. To use it, a player would run a companion script, inputting the color-coded feedback after each guess. The program then recommends the next word expected to provide the most useful information. The project began as a classroom assignment in Assistant Professor Congyu Wu's course. He challenged students to apply information theory to a real-world problem. "What is especially creative is that it transformed a static measurement into a dynamic solution," Wu says. The team compared their entropy-based method with a traditional strategy that prioritizes frequent letters. The entropy approach consistently outperformed it, solving puzzles more efficiently and rarely failing. This work not only offers a winning Wordle tactic but also demonstrates how information theory can optimize practical tasks. It's a powerful reminder that sometimes the best move isn't the most obvious one — it's the one that teaches you the most.
why_it_matters: This work demonstrates that abstract math like information theory can be applied to fun everyday puzzles, encouraging students to see the value in learning STEM concepts and potentially using them to solve larger real-world problems.

background_read: Wordle, the daily word-guessing game created by Welsh software engineer Josh Wardle, became a global sensation in late 2021 and was later acquired by The New York Times for over $1 million.

Claude Shannon, an American mathematician and engineer, founded information theory in 1948 with his landmark paper 'A Mathematical Theory of Communication,' introducing entropy as a measure of uncertainty.
Since then, entropy-based strategies have been used to solve puzzles like Mastermind and even to model decision-making in economics and biology.

The Northeast Journal of Complex Systems is a peer-reviewed academic journal that publishes interdisciplinary research on complex systems, while Binghamton University, part of the State University of New York (SUNY) system, is known for its strong computer science and systems science programs.

The Wordle-solving approach described by Donald Stephens and Congyu Wu shows how a high-level mathematical concept can be turned into a practical tool for a casual game, highlighting the power of applied mathematics in everyday life.

perspectives.description: The entropy strategy shows how a seemingly abstract theory can be turned into a near-perfect solving tool, proving that math isn't just for textbooks—it has real, fun applications. It also underscores the value of student-driven research projects.

perspectives.perspective: Loss of fun and human skill
perspectives.description: Using an algorithm takes the human challenge out of Wordle; the joy of deducing words through intuition and vocabulary is replaced by a script's cold logic. Some argue that the game's simplicity is what made it popular, and automation could reduce its appeal.

The method reveals a deeper truth about problem-solving: the most useful guess is not necessarily the most likely answer, but the one that eliminates the most possibilities. This principle is used in many areas, from medical diagnosis to search engines.

The entropy approach could be adapted to other word games, such as crossword puzzles or even spelling correction in apps. More importantly, it could inspire similar algorithms for decision-making under uncertainty, like financial forecasting or climate modeling.
